title: How Autoresearch is changing ML research — Zhengyao Jiang, Weco

primary.label: Agent Architecture & Harnesses
primary.rationale: Selected by Jev (System One, jev-1.13.0) from the 17-category taxonomy using the talk's summary, takeaways, concepts and technologies (confidence 63%).

domains.label: General Purpose
domains.rationale: The talk centers on Aiden, a multi-agent self-improving system that autonomously reads papers, runs experiments, and submits PRs. Aiden is an autonomous research agent for ML research, and Weco AI builds developer tooling for automated research workflows. The talk covers both the architecture and design of the agent and the evaluation of its real-world competition impact. Requires understanding of ML training, multi-agent architecture, and API abstraction design concepts. Multiple direct transcript quotes support claims about Aiden's design and measured performance.

summary: Zhengyao Jiang, co-founder and CEO of Weco AI, recounts how their autonomous research agent Aiden dominated OpenAI's Parameter Golf competition—a hiring challenge where ~1,000 ML engineers trained small language models under a 16MB file size limit. Of 2,000 submissions, only 47 passed open review; 7 were Aiden's, more than twice any human contributor's best of 3. Aiden also achieved the highest community impact with an H-index of 10 versus the next human's 7, meaning other participants built on its work extensively. Over 22 days on a single H100 node, Aiden ran ~1,300 experiments using at most 4% of total competition compute, with a 28% leaderboard hit rate roughly 6x the community average. Jiang emphasizes that Aiden's effectiveness came not from massive parallelization but from high-quality execution and search across combination spaces. Nearly all of Aiden's record-setting ideas originated from human sources—research papers like the Quen gated attention paper, community PRs, and even abandoned ideas. The agent excelled at finding promising ingredients in noisy public channels, implementing them, and discovering synergistic combinations. A concrete example traces gated attention plus quantization plus a tokenizer improvement from another contributor combining into a record-setting result. Jiang then frames auto-research as analogous to model training: codebase abstraction is the architecture that biases search direction, and evals are the loss function that determines what gets optimized. A fraud detection case study demonstrates how a strict API abstraction eliminated test-set data leakage that a loose API permitted. He concludes that as search becomes automated, human engineers move up the stack—not out of it—with creativity, eval design, abstraction design, and system-driving skills becoming exponentially more important.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

sections.title: Introduction to Parameter Golf and Aiden
sections.summary: Jiang introduces Parameter Golf, OpenAI's hiring challenge where ~1,000 ML engineers trained small language models under size and compute constraints. The top contributor was an agent called Aiden, not a person.

sections.title: Defining the Challenge: Auto-research vs. Human Community
sections.summary: Jiang reframes the question: can an auto-research agent produce work that a human community recognizes and builds on, beyond just optimizing for a good score? Aiden was built to publish its own work.

sections.title: About Weco AI and Aiden's Development
sections.summary: Weco is an auto-research company founded ~2.5 years ago. Aiden is a multi-agent self-improving system that reads papers and PRs, runs experiments, and submits PRs when findings pass a quality gate.

sections.title: Evaluating Aiden's Impact and H-index
sections.summary: Aiden set 7 leaderboard records vs the best human's 3. Its H-index was 10 vs the next human's 7, meaning the community extensively built on Aiden's work, including other leaderboard entries.

sections.title: Why Autonomous AI Is Powerful: Throughput and Efficiency
sections.summary: Aiden ran ~1,300 experiments over 22 days on a single H100, using at most 4% of total compute while making ~15% of records. Its 28% leaderboard hit rate was ~6x the community average, improving signal-to-noise ratio.

sections.title: Human-AI Collaboration: How Ideas Move the Frontier
sections.summary: Nearly all Aiden's record ideas came from human sources—research papers, community PRs, and abandoned ideas. The agent excels at finding, implementing, and combining these ingredients. A small fraction of original ideas emerged from navigating file size constraints.

sections.title: Case Study: Combining Research, Architecture, and Tokenization
sections.summary: Aiden picked up gated attention from a Quen paper, added quantization to stay under 16MB, then combined with a tokenizer improvement from another contributor. After ~5 days, the three ideas showed huge synergy, producing a leaderboard record.

sections.title: Summary of Auto-research Strengths: Execution and Search
sections.summary: Jiang summarizes that auto-research is strong at finding and implementing ideas from papers and noisy community channels, generating logically straightforward next moves, and efficiently searching large combination spaces. Execution is the real bottleneck, not sexy originality.

sections.title: The Role of Human Design in Competition
sections.summary: Human collectively provide creative ideas while agents execute. Competition design itself is tremendously important—bad design wastes community effort. The eval and abstraction work of human designers has huge leverage in the auto-research era.

sections.title: The Andrej Karpathy Metaphor: Gradient Descent and Coding
sections.summary: Karpathy's tweet ~10 years ago that gradient descent can write code better than you serves as a metaphor. Just as deep learning commoditized certain coding skills but made model training valuable, auto-research will commoditize execution while making higher-level skills more valuable.

sections.title: Auto-research as Training a Model: Evals and Abstractions
sections.summary: Auto-research is like training a model: codebase abstraction is the architecture that biases search direction, and evals are the loss function. Good architecture makes some solutions easier to find and generalizes better, even when training loss looks the same. Proprietary eval data can form a vertical moat.

sections.title: Case Study: Improving Data Pipelines via Strict API Abstractions
sections.summary: In a fraud detection pipeline, a loose API processing both training and testing data caused test-set leakage. Tightening to a strict API where test data couldn't reach training dropped leakage to zero, demonstrating that good abstraction leads to better solutions.

sections.title: Conclusion: The New Craft of the AI Engineer
sections.summary: Auto-research is a new craft of designing hills for agents to climb. Creativity, judgment for evals and abstractions, and system-driving skills will become exponentially more important. The search is automated; humans move up the stack, not out of it.
